blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Set out the main supply-side policy measures, trace how each works, and weigh strength against drawbacks.

blocks.heading: The six measures
blocks.text: The syllabus names six measures. Education and training: spending on schools, colleges and workplace training to raise the skills of workers. Labour market reforms: changes to hiring rules and job placement that make it easier for firms to take on workers and for job seekers to find them. Lower direct taxes: cutting income tax and company tax so each hour worked and each Namibian dollar of profit kept pays better. Deregulation: removing rules that raise firms' costs or block new entrants. Improving incentives to work and invest: benefits and tax rules shaped so working and investing pay better. Privatisation: moving a state-owned business into private hands. Japan's apprenticeship reforms show the same measures abroad.

blocks.heading: Two measures traced
blocks.text: Trace a tax cut: the rate of income tax falls from 24% to 18% for a Katutura worker earning N$84 000 a year. Take-home pay rises from N$84 000 - 0.24 x N$84 000 = N$63 840 to N$84 000 - 0.18 x N$84 000 = N$68 880 a year. The reward from an extra hour of work rises, so the worker is more likely to offer overtime, and firms, keeping more profit, may fund new equipment. Trace deregulation with invented figures: suppose opening a small bakery in Windhoek needs 9 permits and 40 days, and the government cuts this to 3 permits and 10 days. Starting up becomes cheaper and quicker, so more new firms are likely to enter.

blocks.heading: Strength, drawback and a caution on privatisation
blocks.text: The main strength is that measures such as training raise capacity at the root, and the gains persist for a working life, in Vietnam as in Namibia. The main drawback is speed: the measures act slowly, so a government facing a problem now tends to reach for other policies first. The gains also depend on execution, since a poorly taught course adds little and a tax cut may be saved rather than invested. Privatisation carries its own caution: a private owner tends to watch costs and customers more keenly, but where the state-owned firm had no rival, the new owner may simply inherit that same position, so the expected gains may go missing.

blocks.text: The aims these measures serve belong to topic 4.2; the tax measures reappear in topic 4.3, and the productivity of firms is the ground of topic 3.6.
